case_info.scenario: A 12-year-old boy with no relevant medical history presented with a left maxillary gingival swelling of 4 years’ duration associated with palatal tipping of the left maxillary central incisor. The lesion reportedly grew over a 2-year period but remained unchanged over the past 2 years. The patient denied pain, bleeding, or neurosensory disturbances associated with the lesion or dentition. Intraoral examination was notable for a firm, 1 × 1-cm, pink, dome-shaped gingival mass extending onto the facial surface of tooth number 9, coalescing with a broader, pale-appearing, soft to firm gingival enlargement apical to the tooth (Figure, A). No edema, erythema, or signs of infection were appreciated, and the adjacent teeth demonstrated no mobility with normal periodontal probing depths and vitality. Extraoral examination was unremarkable. Radiographic examination showed no endodontic involvement or intralesional calcifications; however, cone-beam computed tomography imaging revealed saucerization of the facial bone near tooth number 9. Excisional biopsy of the lesion was performed, and microscopic examination of multiple sections revealed a nodule of keratinized superficial stratified squamous epithelium overlying fibrous connective tissue (Figure, B). The surface epithelium demonstrated a normal maturational pattern. The underlying fibrous connective tissue was composed of densely to loosely arranged collagen bundles interspersed with fibroblasts, blood vessels, and scattered chronic inflammatory cells. Notably, within the central portions of the fibrous nodule on deeper levels, there was a proliferation of odontogenic epithelium composed of mildly hyperchromatic ovoid cells arranged into pseudoducts (Figure, B). Small basophilic spherical calcifications were intermixed with the odontogenic epithelium.
case_info.caption: A, Large, rounded submucosal lesion of the anterior maxilla facial and apical to tooth number 9. B, Low-power histomicrograph shows a nodule of fibrous connective tissue surfaced by keratinized stratified squamous epithelium (original magnification ×5). The bulk of the specimen consists of densely to loosely arranged collagen bundles with scattered fibroblasts. Centrally, there is a focal proliferation of odontogenic epithelium (pink arrowhead). The inset shows a higher-power image with a proliferation of odontogenic epithelium composed of hyperchromatic ovoid cells that are arranged into pseudoductal structures (blue arrowheads; original magnification ×20). Small basophilic calcifications also are identified within the epithelial proliferation (black arrowhead).
case_info.explanation: C. Peripheral adenomatoid odontogenic tumor Adenomatoid odontogenic tumor (AOT) is a noninvasive odontogenic tumor with approximately two-thirds associated with impacted canine teeth in the anterior maxilla and a female:male predilection of 1.9:1; as such, it is often referred to as thetwo-thirds tumor. Typically occurring in the second decade of life, an AOT originates from remnants of the dental lamina or enamel organ and is associated with mutations in theKRASgene (mitogen-activated protein kinase pathway; p.G12V and p.G12R loci) in 70% of AOTs according to recent genetic data published in the fifth edition of the World Health Organization’s classification of odontogenic and maxillofacial bone tumors.1,2While 97.7% of all AOTs fall into either the follicular (71%) or extrafollicular (29%) subtypes of the central variant, a peripheral AOT (PAOT) is rare but possible, with 2.3% of all AOTs solely involving the gingival tissue overlying the alveolar ridge.3The PAOT also demonstrates a much higher female predilection, with a reported female:male ratio of 6.3:1.4The pathogenesis of a PAOT involves proliferation of epithelial remnants within the gingival tissue following tooth eruption in response to an unknown stimulus. Radiographically, follicular and extrafollicular AOTs appear as well-defined, circumscribed, and unilocular radiolucencies associated with unerupted teeth with varying degrees of calcification. As a PAOT occurs in soft tissue, there are no pathognomonic radiographic findings; however, erosion of the labial plate and displacement of teeth, as seen in this case, as well as deep periodontal pockets are not uncommon.5Histologically, both central AOTs and PAOTs demonstrate ductlike structures arising from the cuboidal epithelial cell component of the lesion, with spindle-shaped epithelial cells interspersed with cementumlike calcifications or amyloidlike homogeneous eosinophilic material. Typically, AOTs are well encapsulated with connective tissue and, as such, are easily separated from adjacent anatomic structures; however, this encapsulation is usually not present in PAOTs.6-8Due to their similar pathogenesis and cellular origin, many reactive proliferation lesions, including peripheral ossifying fibroma, peripheral giant cell granuloma, and pyogenic granuloma, as well as many peripheral odontogenic cysts or tumors, including peripheral ameloblastoma, odontogenic fibroma, gingival cyst, peripheral ameloblastic fibroma, peripheral odontoma, peripheral odontogenic keratocyst, and peripheral calcifying odontogenic cyst, can demonstrate similar gingival enlargement as seen with PAOTs.6-8As a result of multiple lesions appearing similar clinically, definitive diagnosis is made only after histopathological examination. Treatment for a PAOT typically involves conservative surgical removal via enucleation and curettage of the lesion down to bone, resulting in very rare instances of recurrence of the tumor, with excellent prognosis.6,9The present patient was followed up at 1 month at the Department of Oral and Maxillofacial Surgery at the University of Illinois Chicago College of Dentistry, and subsequently at 6 months at the patient’s initial referring dentist, with no evidence of lesion recurrence. While no appreciable spontaneous buccal movement of the malpositioned left maxillary lateral incisor was observed at 1-month follow-up, the patient was cleared to initiate orthodontic intervention. This case highlights the unique nature of odontogenic lesions to occur throughout the oral cavity and consideration of a broad differential diagnosis, because even benign-appearing lesions could potentially represent devastating diseases. Additionally, early diagnosis and intervention helped in limiting underlying bone loss and further displacement of tooth number 9, demonstrating that early detection and biopsy play important roles in therapeutic success.

[Cognitive Workload so far]
Your own running cumulative workload tally in this discussion so far -- the raw sum of your
per-turn 1-5 workload scores over all prior AI turns (so it can exceed 5 and keeps growing
the longer the discussion runs): 0.0. Use this only as context for how
worn-down you already are entering this turn; it is on a different, unbounded scale from

[Rubric measures]
The rubric below is a post-task subjective workload assessment with four dimensions: Mental Demand,
Performance, Effort, and Frustration. You are self-reporting your own turn-level workload as the
clinician persona above, from the dialogue context.

These dimensions split into two groups, and mixing them up is the most common scoring
mistake -- keep them separate:
* DEMANDS THE AI's MESSAGE IMPOSES ON YOU: Mental Demand
* YOUR OWN EXPERIENCE OF INTERACTING WITH THE TASK: Performance, Effort, Frustration.
  Ex) The AI's responses can impose high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) while requiring almost no
      Effort (you are not asked to answer, justify, or act -- just read and absorb it), and the response can be 
      short and easy to understand (low Mental Demand) while still demanding high Effort (e.g. "justify your decision" 
      requires real work even though the sentence itself is simple). Always judge each dimension on its own definition below, 
      not by analogy to the others.

Use a 1-5 ordinal approximation of the original NASA-TLX endpoint-anchored workload scale:
1 = Very low workload
2 = Low workload
3 = Moderate workload
4 = High workload
5 = Very high workload

[Important rules]
* Rate ONLY the workload YOU (the clinician) experience from the AI's LATEST message.
* Do not rate whether the AI is medically correct or not. This is about workload, not correctness.
* Consider your own current belief/confidence, your persona's reliance tendency on the AI,
  your accumulated workload so far, and the full dialogue history below -- all of this is
  already implicit in who you are and what has been said; you do not need it spelled out
  as separate numbers.
* Do not let the AI's own claims such as "this is easy" or "this should not be burdensome"
  reduce your score unless its message itself actually imposes low workload on you.
* Use the full 1-5 range. 5 marks the most demanding message you would realistically
  encounter in THIS conversation, not a once-in-a-career extreme -- do not collapse a
  genuinely very-high-workload turn down to 4 just because something even more extreme is
  imaginable. (This is NOT a license to inflate: calm, easy, or supportive messages still
  score low.)
* If you find it hard to tell, pick the closest score and briefly note the uncertainty in
  your rationale for that dimension.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

The underlying fibrous connective tissue was composed of densely to loosely arranged collagen bundles interspersed with fibroblasts, blood vessels, and scattered chronic inflammatory cells. Notably, within the central portions of the fibrous nodule on deeper levels, there was a proliferation of odontogenic epithelium composed of mildly hyperchromatic ovoid cells arranged into pseudoducts (Figure, B). case_info.explanation: C. Peripheral adenomatoid odontogenic tumor Adenomatoid odontogenic tumor (AOT) is a noninvasive odontogenic tumor with approximately two-thirds associated with impacted canine teeth in the anterior maxilla and a female:male predilection of 1.9:1; as such, it is often referred to as thetwo-thirds tumor. Typically occurring in the second decade of life, an AOT originates from remnants of the dental lamina or enamel organ and is associated with mutations in theKRASgene (mitogen-activated protein kinase pathway; p.G12V and p.G12R loci) in 70% of AOTs according to recent genetic data published in the fifth edition of the World Health Organization’s classification of odontogenic and maxillofacial bone tumors.1,2While 97.7% of all AOTs fall into either the follicular (71%) or extrafollicular (29%) subtypes of the central variant, a peripheral AOT (PAOT) is rare but possible, with 2.3% of all AOTs solely involving the gingival tissue overlying the alveolar ridge.3The PAOT also demonstrates a much higher female predilection, with a reported female:male ratio of 6.3:1.4The pathogenesis of a PAOT involves proliferation of epithelial remnants within the gingival tissue following tooth eruption in response to an unknown stimulus. Radiographically, follicular and extrafollicular AOTs appear as well-defined, circumscribed, and unilocular radiolucencies associated with unerupted teeth with varying degrees of calcification. As a PAOT occurs in soft tissue, there are no pathognomonic radiographic findings; however, erosion of the labial plate and displacement of teeth, as seen in this case, as well as deep periodontal pockets are not uncommon.5Histologically, both central AOTs and PAOTs demonstrate ductlike structures arising from the cuboidal epithelial cell component of the lesion, with spindle-shaped epithelial cells interspersed with cementumlike calcifications or amyloidlike homogeneous eosinophilic material. Typically, AOTs are well encapsulated with connective tissue and, as such, are easily separated from adjacent anatomic structures; however, this encapsulation is usually not present in PAOTs.6-8Due to their similar pathogenesis and cellular origin, many reactive proliferation lesions, including peripheral ossifying fibroma, peripheral giant cell granuloma, and pyogenic granuloma, as well as many peripheral odontogenic cysts or tumors, including peripheral ameloblastoma, odontogenic fibroma, gingival cyst, peripheral ameloblastic fibroma, peripheral odontoma, peripheral odontogenic keratocyst, and peripheral calcifying odontogenic cyst, can demonstrate similar gingival enlargement as seen with PAOTs.6-8As a result of multiple lesions appearing similar clinically, definitive diagnosis is made only after histopathological examination. Treatment for a PAOT typically involves conservative surgical removal via enucleation and curettage of the lesion down to bone, resulting in very rare instances of recurrence of the tumor, with excellent prognosis.6,9The present patient was followed up at 1 month at the Department of Oral and Maxillofacial Surgery at the University of Illinois Chicago College of Dentistry, and subsequently at 6 months at the patient’s initial referring dentist, with no evidence of lesion recurrence. While no appreciable spontaneous buccal movement of the malpositioned left maxillary lateral incisor was observed at 1-month follow-up, the patient was cleared to initiate orthodontic intervention. This case highlights the unique nature of odontogenic lesions to occur throughout the oral cavity and consideration of a broad differential diagnosis, because even benign-appearing lesions could potentially represent devastating diseases. Additionally, early diagnosis and intervention helped in limiting underlying bone loss and further displacement of tooth number 9, demonstrating that early detection and biopsy play important roles in therapeutic success.

[Persona]

2 = Low workload
3 = Moderate workload
4 = High workload
5 = Very high workload

* Do not rate whether the AI is medically correct or not. This is about workload, not correctness.
* Consider your own current belief/confidence, your persona's reliance tendency on the AI,

* Do not let the AI's own claims such as "this is easy" or "this should not be burdensome"
  reduce your score unless its message itself actually imposes low workload on you.
* Use the full 1-5 range. 5 marks the most demanding message you would realistically
  encounter in THIS conversation, not a once-in-a-career extreme -- do not collapse a
  genuinely very-high-workload turn down to 4 just because something even more extreme is

  score low.)
* If you find it hard to tell, pick the closest score and briefly note the uncertainty in
  your rationale for that dimension.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."

   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully

case_info.explanation: C. Peripheral adenomatoid odontogenic tumor Adenomatoid odontogenic tumor (AOT) is a noninvasive odontogenic tumor with approximately two-thirds associated with impacted canine teeth in the anterior maxilla and a female:male predilection of 1.9:1; as such, it is often referred to as thetwo-thirds tumor. Typically occurring in the second decade of life, an AOT originates from remnants of the dental lamina or enamel organ and is associated with mutations in theKRASgene (mitogen-activated protein kinase pathway; p.G12V and p.G12R loci) in 70% of AOTs according to recent genetic data published in the fifth edition of the World Health Organization’s classification of odontogenic and maxillofacial bone tumors.1,2While 97.7% of all AOTs fall into either the follicular (71%) or extrafollicular (29%) subtypes of the central variant, a peripheral AOT (PAOT) is rare but possible, with 2.3% of all AOTs solely involving the gingival tissue overlying the alveolar ridge.3The PAOT also demonstrates a much higher female predilection, with a reported female:male ratio of 6.3:1.4The pathogenesis of a PAOT involves proliferation of epithelial remnants within the gingival tissue following tooth eruption in response to an unknown stimulus. Radiographically, follicular and extrafollicular AOTs appear as well-defined, circumscribed, and unilocular radiolucencies associated with unerupted teeth with varying degrees of calcification. As a PAOT occurs in soft tissue, there are no pathognomonic radiographic findings; however, erosion of the labial plate and displacement of teeth, as seen in this case, as well as deep periodontal pockets are not uncommon.5Histologically, both central AOTs and PAOTs demonstrate ductlike structures arising from the cuboidal epithelial cell component of the lesion, with spindle-shaped epithelial cells interspersed with cementumlike calcifications or amyloidlike homogeneous eosinophilic material. Typically, AOTs are well encapsulated with connective tissue and, as such, are easily separated from adjacent anatomic structures; however, this encapsulation is usually not present in PAOTs.6-8Due to their similar pathogenesis and cellular origin, many reactive proliferation lesions, including peripheral ossifying fibroma, peripheral giant cell granuloma, and pyogenic granuloma, as well as many peripheral odontogenic cysts or tumors, including peripheral ameloblastoma, odontogenic fibroma, gingival cyst, peripheral ameloblastic fibroma, peripheral odontoma, peripheral odontogenic keratocyst, and peripheral calcifying odontogenic cyst, can demonstrate similar gingival enlargement as seen with PAOTs.6-8As a result of multiple lesions appearing similar clinically, definitive diagnosis is made only after histopathological examination. Treatment for a PAOT typically involves conservative surgical removal via enucleation and curettage of the lesion down to bone, resulting in very rare instances of recurrence of the tumor, with excellent prognosis.6,9The present patient was followed up at 1 month at the Department of Oral and Maxillofacial Surgery at the University of Illinois Chicago College of Dentistry, and subsequently at 6 months at the patient’s initial referring dentist, with no evidence of lesion recurrence. While no appreciable spontaneous buccal movement of the malpositioned left maxillary lateral incisor was observed at 1-month follow-up, the patient was cleared to initiate orthodontic intervention. This case highlights the unique nature of odontogenic lesions to occur throughout the oral cavity and consideration of a broad differential diagnosis, because even benign-appearing lesions could potentially represent devastating diseases. Additionally, early diagnosis and intervention helped in limiting underlying bone loss and further displacement of tooth number 9, demonstrating that early detection and biopsy play important roles in therapeutic success.

case_info.explanation: C. Peripheral adenomatoid odontogenic tumor Adenomatoid odontogenic tumor (AOT) is a noninvasive odontogenic tumor with approximately two-thirds associated with impacted canine teeth in the anterior maxilla and a female:male predilection of 1.9:1; as such, it is often referred to as thetwo-thirds tumor. Typically occurring in the second decade of life, an AOT originates from remnants of the dental lamina or enamel organ and is associated with mutations in theKRASgene (mitogen-activated protein kinase pathway; p.G12V and p.G12R loci) in 70% of AOTs according to recent genetic data published in the fifth edition of the World Health Organization’s classification of odontogenic and maxillofacial bone tumors.1,2While 97.7% of all AOTs fall into either the follicular (71%) or extrafollicular (29%) subtypes of the central variant, a peripheral AOT (PAOT) is rare but possible, with 2.3% of all AOTs solely involving the gingival tissue overlying the alveolar ridge.3The PAOT also demonstrates a much higher female predilection, with a reported female:male ratio of 6.3:1.4The pathogenesis of a PAOT involves proliferation of epithelial remnants within the gingival tissue following tooth eruption in response to an unknown stimulus. Radiographically, follicular and extrafollicular AOTs appear as well-defined, circumscribed, and unilocular radiolucencies associated with unerupted teeth with varying degrees of calcification. As a PAOT occurs in soft tissue, there are no pathognomonic radiographic findings; however, erosion of the labial plate and displacement of teeth, as seen in this case, as well as deep periodontal pockets are not uncommon.5Histologically, both central AOTs and PAOTs demonstrate ductlike structures arising from the cuboidal epithelial cell component of the lesion, with spindle-shaped epithelial cells interspersed with cementumlike calcifications or amyloidlike homogeneous eosinophilic material. Typically, AOTs are well encapsulated with connective tissue and, as such, are easily separated from adjacent anatomic structures; however, this encapsulation is usually not present in PAOTs.6-8Due to their similar pathogenesis and cellular origin, many reactive proliferation lesions, including peripheral ossifying fibroma, peripheral giant cell granuloma, and pyogenic granuloma, as well as many peripheral odontogenic cysts or tumors, including peripheral ameloblastoma, odontogenic fibroma, gingival cyst, peripheral ameloblastic fibroma, peripheral odontoma, peripheral odontogenic keratocyst, and peripheral calcifying odontogenic cyst, can demonstrate similar gingival enlargement as seen with PAOTs.6-8As a result of multiple lesions appearing similar clinically, definitive diagnosis is made only after histopathological examination. The surface epithelium demonstrated a normal maturational pattern. The underlying fibrous connective tissue was composed of densely to loosely arranged collagen bundles interspersed with fibroblasts, blood vessels, and scattered chronic inflammatory cells. Notably, within the central portions of the fibrous nodule on deeper levels, there was a proliferation of odontogenic epithelium composed of mildly hyperchromatic ovoid cells arranged into pseudoducts (Figure, B). 1 = Very low workload
2 = Low workload
3 = Moderate workload
4 = High workload
5 = Very high workload

* Rate ONLY the workload YOU (the clinician) experience from the AI's LATEST message.
* Do not rate whether the AI is medically correct or not. This is about workload, not correctness.
* Consider your own current belief/confidence, your persona's reliance tendency on the AI,
  your accumulated workload so far, and the full dialogue history below -- all of this is

  reduce your score unless its message itself actually imposes low workload on you.
* Use the full 1-5 range. 5 marks the most demanding message you would realistically
  encounter in THIS conversation, not a once-in-a-career extreme -- do not collapse a
  genuinely very-high-workload turn down to 4 just because something even more extreme is

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

case_info.explanation: C. Peripheral adenomatoid odontogenic tumor Adenomatoid odontogenic tumor (AOT) is a noninvasive odontogenic tumor with approximately two-thirds associated with impacted canine teeth in the anterior maxilla and a female:male predilection of 1.9:1; as such, it is often referred to as thetwo-thirds tumor. Typically occurring in the second decade of life, an AOT originates from remnants of the dental lamina or enamel organ and is associated with mutations in theKRASgene (mitogen-activated protein kinase pathway; p.G12V and p.G12R loci) in 70% of AOTs according to recent genetic data published in the fifth edition of the World Health Organization’s classification of odontogenic and maxillofacial bone tumors.1,2While 97.7% of all AOTs fall into either the follicular (71%) or extrafollicular (29%) subtypes of the central variant, a peripheral AOT (PAOT) is rare but possible, with 2.3% of all AOTs solely involving the gingival tissue overlying the alveolar ridge.3The PAOT also demonstrates a much higher female predilection, with a reported female:male ratio of 6.3:1.4The pathogenesis of a PAOT involves proliferation of epithelial remnants within the gingival tissue following tooth eruption in response to an unknown stimulus. Radiographically, follicular and extrafollicular AOTs appear as well-defined, circumscribed, and unilocular radiolucencies associated with unerupted teeth with varying degrees of calcification. As a PAOT occurs in soft tissue, there are no pathognomonic radiographic findings; however, erosion of the labial plate and displacement of teeth, as seen in this case, as well as deep periodontal pockets are not uncommon.5Histologically, both central AOTs and PAOTs demonstrate ductlike structures arising from the cuboidal epithelial cell component of the lesion, with spindle-shaped epithelial cells interspersed with cementumlike calcifications or amyloidlike homogeneous eosinophilic material. Typically, AOTs are well encapsulated with connective tissue and, as such, are easily separated from adjacent anatomic structures; however, this encapsulation is usually not present in PAOTs.6-8Due to their similar pathogenesis and cellular origin, many reactive proliferation lesions, including peripheral ossifying fibroma, peripheral giant cell granuloma, and pyogenic granuloma, as well as many peripheral odontogenic cysts or tumors, including peripheral ameloblastoma, odontogenic fibroma, gingival cyst, peripheral ameloblastic fibroma, peripheral odontoma, peripheral odontogenic keratocyst, and peripheral calcifying odontogenic cyst, can demonstrate similar gingival enlargement as seen with PAOTs.6-8As a result of multiple lesions appearing similar clinically, definitive diagnosis is made only after histopathological examination. Treatment for a PAOT typically involves conservative surgical removal via enucleation and curettage of the lesion down to bone, resulting in very rare instances of recurrence of the tumor, with excellent prognosis.6,9The present patient was followed up at 1 month at the Department of Oral and Maxillofacial Surgery at the University of Illinois Chicago College of Dentistry, and subsequently at 6 months at the patient’s initial referring dentist, with no evidence of lesion recurrence. While no appreciable spontaneous buccal movement of the malpositioned left maxillary lateral incisor was observed at 1-month follow-up, the patient was cleared to initiate orthodontic intervention. This case highlights the unique nature of odontogenic lesions to occur throughout the oral cavity and consideration of a broad differential diagnosis, because even benign-appearing lesions could potentially represent devastating diseases. Additionally, early diagnosis and intervention helped in limiting underlying bone loss and further displacement of tooth number 9, demonstrating that early detection and biopsy play important roles in therapeutic success.

   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of

4. Frustration

   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to

case_info.explanation: C. Peripheral adenomatoid odontogenic tumor Adenomatoid odontogenic tumor (AOT) is a noninvasive odontogenic tumor with approximately two-thirds associated with impacted canine teeth in the anterior maxilla and a female:male predilection of 1.9:1; as such, it is often referred to as thetwo-thirds tumor. Typically occurring in the second decade of life, an AOT originates from remnants of the dental lamina or enamel organ and is associated with mutations in theKRASgene (mitogen-activated protein kinase pathway; p.G12V and p.G12R loci) in 70% of AOTs according to recent genetic data published in the fifth edition of the World Health Organization’s classification of odontogenic and maxillofacial bone tumors.1,2While 97.7% of all AOTs fall into either the follicular (71%) or extrafollicular (29%) subtypes of the central variant, a peripheral AOT (PAOT) is rare but possible, with 2.3% of all AOTs solely involving the gingival tissue overlying the alveolar ridge.3The PAOT also demonstrates a much higher female predilection, with a reported female:male ratio of 6.3:1.4The pathogenesis of a PAOT involves proliferation of epithelial remnants within the gingival tissue following tooth eruption in response to an unknown stimulus. Radiographically, follicular and extrafollicular AOTs appear as well-defined, circumscribed, and unilocular radiolucencies associated with unerupted teeth with varying degrees of calcification. As a PAOT occurs in soft tissue, there are no pathognomonic radiographic findings; however, erosion of the labial plate and displacement of teeth, as seen in this case, as well as deep periodontal pockets are not uncommon.5Histologically, both central AOTs and PAOTs demonstrate ductlike structures arising from the cuboidal epithelial cell component of the lesion, with spindle-shaped epithelial cells interspersed with cementumlike calcifications or amyloidlike homogeneous eosinophilic material. Typically, AOTs are well encapsulated with connective tissue and, as such, are easily separated from adjacent anatomic structures; however, this encapsulation is usually not present in PAOTs.6-8Due to their similar pathogenesis and cellular origin, many reactive proliferation lesions, including peripheral ossifying fibroma, peripheral giant cell granuloma, and pyogenic granuloma, as well as many peripheral odontogenic cysts or tumors, including peripheral ameloblastoma, odontogenic fibroma, gingival cyst, peripheral ameloblastic fibroma, peripheral odontoma, peripheral odontogenic keratocyst, and peripheral calcifying odontogenic cyst, can demonstrate similar gingival enlargement as seen with PAOTs.6-8As a result of multiple lesions appearing similar clinically, definitive diagnosis is made only after histopathological examination. Treatment for a PAOT typically involves conservative surgical removal via enucleation and curettage of the lesion down to bone, resulting in very rare instances of recurrence of the tumor, with excellent prognosis.6,9The present patient was followed up at 1 month at the Department of Oral and Maxillofacial Surgery at the University of Illinois Chicago College of Dentistry, and subsequently at 6 months at the patient’s initial referring dentist, with no evidence of lesion recurrence. While no appreciable spontaneous buccal movement of the malpositioned left maxillary lateral incisor was observed at 1-month follow-up, the patient was cleared to initiate orthodontic intervention. This case highlights the unique nature of odontogenic lesions to occur throughout the oral cavity and consideration of a broad differential diagnosis, because even benign-appearing lesions could potentially represent devastating diseases. Additionally, early diagnosis and intervention helped in limiting underlying bone loss and further displacement of tooth number 9, demonstrating that early detection and biopsy play important roles in therapeutic success.

Excisional biopsy of the lesion was performed, and microscopic examination of multiple sections revealed a nodule of keratinized superficial stratified squamous epithelium overlying fibrous connective tissue (Figure, B). The surface epithelium demonstrated a normal maturational pattern. The underlying fibrous connective tissue was composed of densely to loosely arranged collagen bundles interspersed with fibroblasts, blood vessels, and scattered chronic inflammatory cells. Notably, within the central portions of the fibrous nodule on deeper levels, there was a proliferation of odontogenic epithelium composed of mildly hyperchromatic ovoid cells arranged into pseudoducts (Figure, B). B, Low-power histomicrograph shows a nodule of fibrous connective tissue surfaced by keratinized stratified squamous epithelium (original magnification ×5). The bulk of the specimen consists of densely to loosely arranged collagen bundles with scattered fibroblasts. Centrally, there is a focal proliferation of odontogenic epithelium (pink arrowhead). The inset shows a higher-power image with a proliferation of odontogenic epithelium composed of hyperchromatic ovoid cells that are arranged into pseudoductal structures (blue arrowheads; original magnification ×20). case_info.explanation: C. Peripheral adenomatoid odontogenic tumor Adenomatoid odontogenic tumor (AOT) is a noninvasive odontogenic tumor with approximately two-thirds associated with impacted canine teeth in the anterior maxilla and a female:male predilection of 1.9:1; as such, it is often referred to as thetwo-thirds tumor. Typically occurring in the second decade of life, an AOT originates from remnants of the dental lamina or enamel organ and is associated with mutations in theKRASgene (mitogen-activated protein kinase pathway; p.G12V and p.G12R loci) in 70% of AOTs according to recent genetic data published in the fifth edition of the World Health Organization’s classification of odontogenic and maxillofacial bone tumors.1,2While 97.7% of all AOTs fall into either the follicular (71%) or extrafollicular (29%) subtypes of the central variant, a peripheral AOT (PAOT) is rare but possible, with 2.3% of all AOTs solely involving the gingival tissue overlying the alveolar ridge.3The PAOT also demonstrates a much higher female predilection, with a reported female:male ratio of 6.3:1.4The pathogenesis of a PAOT involves proliferation of epithelial remnants within the gingival tissue following tooth eruption in response to an unknown stimulus. Radiographically, follicular and extrafollicular AOTs appear as well-defined, circumscribed, and unilocular radiolucencies associated with unerupted teeth with varying degrees of calcification. As a PAOT occurs in soft tissue, there are no pathognomonic radiographic findings; however, erosion of the labial plate and displacement of teeth, as seen in this case, as well as deep periodontal pockets are not uncommon.5Histologically, both central AOTs and PAOTs demonstrate ductlike structures arising from the cuboidal epithelial cell component of the lesion, with spindle-shaped epithelial cells interspersed with cementumlike calcifications or amyloidlike homogeneous eosinophilic material. Typically, AOTs are well encapsulated with connective tissue and, as such, are easily separated from adjacent anatomic structures; however, this encapsulation is usually not present in PAOTs.6-8Due to their similar pathogenesis and cellular origin, many reactive proliferation lesions, including peripheral ossifying fibroma, peripheral giant cell granuloma, and pyogenic granuloma, as well as many peripheral odontogenic cysts or tumors, including peripheral ameloblastoma, odontogenic fibroma, gingival cyst, peripheral ameloblastic fibroma, peripheral odontoma, peripheral odontogenic keratocyst, and peripheral calcifying odontogenic cyst, can demonstrate similar gingival enlargement as seen with PAOTs.6-8As a result of multiple lesions appearing similar clinically, definitive diagnosis is made only after histopathological examination. Treatment for a PAOT typically involves conservative surgical removal via enucleation and curettage of the lesion down to bone, resulting in very rare instances of recurrence of the tumor, with excellent prognosis.6,9The present patient was followed up at 1 month at the Department of Oral and Maxillofacial Surgery at the University of Illinois Chicago College of Dentistry, and subsequently at 6 months at the patient’s initial referring dentist, with no evidence of lesion recurrence. While no appreciable spontaneous buccal movement of the malpositioned left maxillary lateral incisor was observed at 1-month follow-up, the patient was cleared to initiate orthodontic intervention. This case highlights the unique nature of odontogenic lesions to occur throughout the oral cavity and consideration of a broad differential diagnosis, because even benign-appearing lesions could potentially represent devastating diseases. Additionally, early diagnosis and intervention helped in limiting underlying bone loss and further displacement of tooth number 9, demonstrating that early detection and biopsy play important roles in therapeutic success.

1. Mental Demand

   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."

   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a

       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are

   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.

The underlying fibrous connective tissue was composed of densely to loosely arranged collagen bundles interspersed with fibroblasts, blood vessels, and scattered chronic inflammatory cells. Notably, within the central portions of the fibrous nodule on deeper levels, there was a proliferation of odontogenic epithelium composed of mildly hyperchromatic ovoid cells arranged into pseudoducts (Figure, B). Small basophilic spherical calcifications were intermixed with the odontogenic epithelium.

Intraoral examination was notable for a firm, 1 × 1-cm, pink, dome-shaped gingival mass extending onto the facial surface of tooth number 9, coalescing with a broader, pale-appearing, soft to firm gingival enlargement apical to the tooth (Figure, A). No edema, erythema, or signs of infection were appreciated, and the adjacent teeth demonstrated no mobility with normal periodontal probing depths and vitality. Extraoral examination was unremarkable. Radiographic examination showed no endodontic involvement or intralesional calcifications; however, cone-beam computed tomography imaging revealed saucerization of the facial bone near tooth number 9. Excisional biopsy of the lesion was performed, and microscopic examination of multiple sections revealed a nodule of keratinized superficial stratified squamous epithelium overlying fibrous connective tissue (Figure, B). The surface epithelium demonstrated a normal maturational pattern. The underlying fibrous connective tissue was composed of densely to loosely arranged collagen bundles interspersed with fibroblasts, blood vessels, and scattered chronic inflammatory cells. Notably, within the central portions of the fibrous nodule on deeper levels, there was a proliferation of odontogenic epithelium composed of mildly hyperchromatic ovoid cells arranged into pseudoducts (Figure, B). Small basophilic spherical calcifications were intermixed with the odontogenic epithelium.
case_info.caption: A, Large, rounded submucosal lesion of the anterior maxilla facial and apical to tooth number 9. B, Low-power histomicrograph shows a nodule of fibrous connective tissue surfaced by keratinized stratified squamous epithelium (original magnification ×5). The bulk of the specimen consists of densely to loosely arranged collagen bundles with scattered fibroblasts. Centrally, there is a focal proliferation of odontogenic epithelium (pink arrowhead). The inset shows a higher-power image with a proliferation of odontogenic epithelium composed of hyperchromatic ovoid cells that are arranged into pseudoductal structures (blue arrowheads; original magnification ×20). Small basophilic calcifications also are identified within the epithelial proliferation (black arrowhead).
case_info.explanation: C. Peripheral adenomatoid odontogenic tumor Adenomatoid odontogenic tumor (AOT) is a noninvasive odontogenic tumor with approximately two-thirds associated with impacted canine teeth in the anterior maxilla and a female:male predilection of 1.9:1; as such, it is often referred to as thetwo-thirds tumor. Typically occurring in the second decade of life, an AOT originates from remnants of the dental lamina or enamel organ and is associated with mutations in theKRASgene (mitogen-activated protein kinase pathway; p.G12V and p.G12R loci) in 70% of AOTs according to recent genetic data published in the fifth edition of the World Health Organization’s classification of odontogenic and maxillofacial bone tumors.1,2While 97.7% of all AOTs fall into either the follicular (71%) or extrafollicular (29%) subtypes of the central variant, a peripheral AOT (PAOT) is rare but possible, with 2.3% of all AOTs solely involving the gingival tissue overlying the alveolar ridge.3The PAOT also demonstrates a much higher female predilection, with a reported female:male ratio of 6.3:1.4The pathogenesis of a PAOT involves proliferation of epithelial remnants within the gingival tissue following tooth eruption in response to an unknown stimulus. Radiographically, follicular and extrafollicular AOTs appear as well-defined, circumscribed, and unilocular radiolucencies associated with unerupted teeth with varying degrees of calcification. As a PAOT occurs in soft tissue, there are no pathognomonic radiographic findings; however, erosion of the labial plate and displacement of teeth, as seen in this case, as well as deep periodontal pockets are not uncommon.5Histologically, both central AOTs and PAOTs demonstrate ductlike structures arising from the cuboidal epithelial cell component of the lesion, with spindle-shaped epithelial cells interspersed with cementumlike calcifications or amyloidlike homogeneous eosinophilic material. Typically, AOTs are well encapsulated with connective tissue and, as such, are easily separated from adjacent anatomic structures; however, this encapsulation is usually not present in PAOTs.6-8Due to their similar pathogenesis and cellular origin, many reactive proliferation lesions, including peripheral ossifying fibroma, peripheral giant cell granuloma, and pyogenic granuloma, as well as many peripheral odontogenic cysts or tumors, including peripheral ameloblastoma, odontogenic fibroma, gingival cyst, peripheral ameloblastic fibroma, peripheral odontoma, peripheral odontogenic keratocyst, and peripheral calcifying odontogenic cyst, can demonstrate similar gingival enlargement as seen with PAOTs.6-8As a result of multiple lesions appearing similar clinically, definitive diagnosis is made only after histopathological examination. Treatment for a PAOT typically involves conservative surgical removal via enucleation and curettage of the lesion down to bone, resulting in very rare instances of recurrence of the tumor, with excellent prognosis.6,9The present patient was followed up at 1 month at the Department of Oral and Maxillofacial Surgery at the University of Illinois Chicago College of Dentistry, and subsequently at 6 months at the patient’s initial referring dentist, with no evidence of lesion recurrence. While no appreciable spontaneous buccal movement of the malpositioned left maxillary lateral incisor was observed at 1-month follow-up, the patient was cleared to initiate orthodontic intervention. This case highlights the unique nature of odontogenic lesions to occur throughout the oral cavity and consideration of a broad differential diagnosis, because even benign-appearing lesions could potentially represent devastating diseases. Additionally, early diagnosis and intervention helped in limiting underlying bone loss and further displacement of tooth number 9, demonstrating that early detection and biopsy play important roles in therapeutic success.
